onze vaderen in de 16e eeuw bestonden, trokken Schweizer en Scholten
mij als vanzelf het sterkst aan. Toch kwam mijn levenskeus eerst door
een prijsvraag van de Groninger theologische faculteit, waarop ik een
goedgekeurd antwoord inzond tot vaste beslissing. Zelf had ik op die
prijsvraag ganschelijk niet gelet, en het was de hoogleeraar de Vries,
die er bij mij op aandrong, dat ik een antwoord wagen zou. Die prijs-
vraag nu liep over het kerkbegrip van Calvijn en van den Poolschen
geleerde Ivan Lasky, gemeenlijk Johannes à Lasco genoemd. Zoo kwam
ik vanzelf bij Calvijn thuis, en daar Kerk en Staat in de opvatting van
de 16e eeuw zoo innig nauw saamhingen, lokten mijn studiën mij reeds
toen, tot op zekere hoogte, naar het politiek terrein.
Maar ook zoo ontbrak toch nog alle aanraking met het politieke
leven. Ik bleef theoloog zonder meer, en voelde nog geen de minste aan-
drift om wat in de 16e eeuw onze vaderen op politiek gebied bezielde, te
doen herleven. Van Groen van Prinsterer had ik nog nimmer iets gelezen, en
het sterkst nog sprak mijn politieke neiging zich uit, toen ik in 1853 voor de
actie tegen de Bisschoppelijke hierarchie letterlijk opvlamde. Zelfs te Beesd
ging van mij als predikant geen andere actie uit dan in conservatieve
richting. Het is dan ook niet anders dan het contact met het leven, dat
nog in de dusgenaamde Nachtschool ritselde, waardoor ik de ondoen-
lijkheid inzag, eenerzijds om theologie en politiek van elkander te scheiden,
en anderzijds om 1789 in plaats van 1578 als uitgangspunt voor de histo-
risch-politieke lijn te kiezen. Het waren niet de bezielingen van den Reveil,
en ook niet de Supranaturalistische vindingen, die mij dit contact met het
historische leven gaven. Dit contact kwam uit het overblijfsel der aloude
„Gezelschappen”, met hun breeden aanhang. In die Gereformeerde krin-
gen had men nog een eigen litteratuur, en die litteratuur sprak nog theologisch
en politiek als onafscheidelijk één. Alleen maar scheen het theologisch-
politieke leven in die kringen te verouderen. Wat Owen er nog als ’t
klaarste licht over ontstak, geraakte uit zijn tijd; en al had Alexander
Comrie het pogen te verjongen, toch was ook hij met zijn tijd te weinig
medegegaan. Dibbets, Bechthold en Kûhler, het driemanschap dat te Am-
sterdam destijds, met Grosheide, onze stoere Gereformeerden nog poogde
te redden, spraken het telkens weer uit, dat er verheldering van inzicht en
vooral verjongde toepassing noodig was, zou de kern van ons volk zijn
innerlijke kracht ook in de nieuwgeboren toestanden onverzwakt behouden
kunnen. Ons Calvinistisch volk toch is nimmer tevreden geweest met stichtelijk
vermaan. Het heeft nimmer kunnen rusten, eer het zich sterk gevoelde in een
eigen levens- en wereldbeschouwing, gelijk die met breeden uitslag in Gods
Woord geteekend lag. Reeds in de dagen van Dordt was deze kern van ons
critical_translation:
our fathers [Dutch: vaderen] existed in the 16th century, Schweizer [Dutch: Schweizer] and Scholten [Dutch: Scholten] drew me most strongly as if by themselves. Yet [Dutch: Toch] came my life's choice first through a prize question of the Groningen [Dutch: Groninger] theological faculty, whereupon I submitted an approved answer unto firm decision. Myself had I not at all paid attention to that prize question, and it was Professor [Dutch: hoogleeraar] de Vries [Dutch: de Vries], who urged me thereon, that I should venture an answer. That prize question now concerned the concept of the church [Dutch: kerkbegrip] of Calvin [Dutch: Calvijn] and of the Polish [Dutch: Poolschen] scholar [Dutch: geleerde] Ivan Lasky [Dutch: Ivan Lasky], commonly called Johannes à Lasco [Dutch: Johannes à Lasco]. Thus came I of myself to Calvin's [Dutch: Calvijn] home, and since Church [Dutch: Kerk] and State [Dutch: Staat] in the conception of the 16th century so intimately closely hung together, my studies already then lured me, to a certain extent, towards the political terrain.
But also thus yet [Dutch: toch] still lacked all contact with political life. I remained theologian without more, and felt yet not the least impulse to revive what in the 16th century animated our fathers [Dutch: vaderen] in the political domain. Of Groen van Prinsterer [Dutch: Groen van Prinsterer] had I yet never read anything, and most strongly yet expressed itself my political inclination, when I in 1853 for the action against the Episcopal [Dutch: Bisschoppelijke] hierarchy literally flared up. Even at Beesd [Dutch: Beesd] went forth from me as pastor [Dutch: predikant] no other action than in conservative direction. It is then also nothing other than the contact with life, that yet rustled in the so-called Night School [Dutch: Nachtschool], whereby I perceived the impossibility, on the one hand to separate theology and politics from one another, and on the other hand to choose 1789 instead of 1578 as starting point for the historical-political line. It was not the inspirations of the Reveil [Dutch: Reveil], and also not the Supranaturalistic [Dutch: Supranaturalistische] inventions, that gave me this contact with historical life. This contact came from the remnant of the ancient "Societies" [Dutch: Gezelschappen], with their broad following. In those Reformed [Dutch: Gereformeerde] circles one still had an own literature, and that literature yet spoke theologically and politically as inseparably one. Only did the theological-political life in those circles seem to age. What Owen [Dutch: Owen] yet ignited over it as the clearest light, fell out of its time; and although Alexander Comrie [Dutch: Alexander Comrie] had attempted to rejuvenate it, yet [Dutch: toch] had he also too little kept pace with his time. Dibbets [Dutch: Dibbets], Bechthold [Dutch: Bechthold] and Kûhler [Dutch: Kûhler], the triumvirate that at Amsterdam [Dutch: Amsterdam] at that time, with Grosheide [Dutch: Grosheide], yet sought to save our sturdy Reformed [Dutch: Gereformeerden], expressed it again and again, that clarification of insight and especially rejuvenated application was necessary, should the core of our people [Dutch: volk] be able to retain its inner strength also in the newborn conditions unweakened. Our Calvinistic [Dutch: Calvinistisch] people [Dutch: volk] yet [Dutch: toch] has never been content with edifying admonition. It has never been able to rest, ere it felt itself strong in an own life- and worldview [Dutch: levens- en wereldbeschouwing], as that with broad outcome lay drawn in God's Word [Dutch: Woord]. Already in the days of Dort [Dutch: Dordt] was this core of ours

Nevertheless, my life's choice was first determined by a prize question from the Groningen theological faculty, whereupon I submitted an approved answer which led to a firm decision. I myself had paid no heed whatsoever to that prize question, and it was Professor de Vries who urged me to venture an answer thereto. That prize question concerned, namely, the concept of the church held by Calvin and by the Polish scholar Ivan Lasky, commonly called Johannes à Lasco. Thus I naturally found my way to Calvin's thought, and since Church and State, in the conception of the sixteenth century, were so intimately intertwined, my studies even then, to a certain extent, lured me towards the political domain.\nYet even so, all contact with political life was still wanting. I remained merely a theologian, and felt not the slightest impulse to revive that which animated our fathers in the political domain in the sixteenth century. Of Groen van Prinsterer I had, as yet, read nothing; and my political inclination expressed itself most strongly when, in 1853, I literally ignited with fervor for the action against the Episcopal hierarchy. Even at Beesd, no other action emanated from me as pastor than in a conservative direction. It was, therefore, none other than the contact with life, which still stirred within the so-called Night School, whereby I perceived the impossibility, on the one hand, to separate theology and politics from one another, and on the other, to choose 1789 instead of 1578 as the starting point for the historical-political trajectory. It was neither the inspirations of the Reveil nor the Supranaturalistic inventions that granted me this contact with historical life. This contact arose from the remnant of the ancient 'Societies,' with their wide following. In those Reformed circles, a distinct literature was still maintained, and that literature yet spoke theologically and politically as an inseparable unity. Only, however, did the theological-political life in those circles appear to be growing antiquated. What Owen had once ignited therein as the clearest light, had fallen out of its time; and although Alexander Comrie had attempted to rejuvenate it, nevertheless, he too had failed to keep sufficient pace with his era. Dibbets, Bechthold, and Kûhler, the triumvirate who, at Amsterdam in that era, with Grosheide, still sought to preserve our sturdy Reformed adherents, repeatedly declared that a clarification of insight and, above all, a rejuvenated application were necessary, if the core of our people were to retain its inner strength, unweakened, even amidst the newly emergent conditions. Our Calvinistic people has, nevertheless, never been content with mere edifying admonition. It has never been able to rest until it felt itself strong in a distinct life- and world-and-life view, such as that which, with broad outcome, lay delineated in God's Word. Already in the days of Dort, this core of our people...",
